 The best laptop power banks are a must-buy when you're working away from a power socket. After all, even the best laptops for photo editing won't run on battery forever. And with governments telling us all to stock up on food and prepare for power outages, a power bank is a great way of ensuring you can keep vital devices going for a few days if the mains electricity fails to flow.
 But, the best iPhone power banks won't be powerful enough to do the job. Instead, you'll need a power bank with at least 18,000mAh capacity, as well as the right ports to connect to your specific laptop.
 As an added bonus, with a power bank this powerful, you'll be able to charge your cameras, tablets, phones,and other devices too. To find you the best model for your needs, we've put our experts to work. They've been testing and reviewing power banks, as well as using them within their own workflows, in order to compile this list of the absolute best.

 The DJI Power 1000 is a rugged, high-capacity power station designed with drone users in mind. With 1,024Wh of capacity and 2,200W continuous output (4,400W peak), it provides ample power for charging multiple drone batteries, cameras, and other essential gear on location. The two USB-C ports (140W each) allow for fast charging, while the SDC and SDC Lite ports support DJI’s proprietary adapters for even more efficient drone charging.
 Weighing 13kg, the Power 1000 is not the lightest option, but its sturdy build and rounded handles make it easy to carry. The clear display offers essential battery information, though it lacks smart features like an app or battery health monitoring. Additionally, there’s no built-in light or wireless charging, which could be a drawback for some users.
 Despite these limitations, the DJI Power 1000 excels at providing reliable, high-wattage power for drone operators and creatives working off-grid. Whether you're filming in remote locations or need a dependable backup power source, this station delivers efficient, high-speed charging for DJI drones and other kit.

 Want the best power bank that will fit in your pocket? We reckon that's the UGREEN 300W 48,000mAh; a robust and high-capacity portable charger designed for users seeking extensive device charging capabilities.
 This power bank stands out for two main reasons. One is its impressive 48,000mAh capacity, which makes it capable of charging an iPhone 15 Pro nearly 11 times. The second is its ability to charge up to five devices at the same time, with a maximum output of 300W. That makes it particularly well-suited for camping trips, weekend hikes, or emergency power situations.
 Despite its somewhat hefty weight of 1.86 kg, the power bank features a sleek design with high-quality materials, including a low-light display that provides real-time information about battery level and power input/output. Equipped with two USB-A ports and three USB-C ports, the power bank offers versatile charging options.
 It's likely to last you a while too; Ugreen claims the device will retain 80% of its capacity after 3,000 charge cycles. However, our reviewer also noted a few drawbacks, such as its heavy weight, the lack of an included charging plug, and variable charging speeds depending on the cables used.

Capable of 145W power split across its USB ports, with one 100W capable USB-C, it's ready for all your devices that can be fast charged, as well as laptops that need lots of juice, and it's also future-proofed for those devices that haven't come along yet. With enough capacity to charge your phone several times over, or run your camera and accessories off while on long shoots away from a constant power supply.
 However it isn't the only 25,000mAh capacity power bank on the market, so if you don't need its fast charging powers then you can get cheaper and lighter options elsewhere (or from UGREEN themselves), and the complex and varying power outputs might just be enough to put a lot of people off.

 You don't really need to have an informative screen on your power bank, but the Anker Prime power bank has the easiest power percentage and countdown timer for charging/discharging the battery I have used yet. And knowing exactly how fast my laptop is charging is both just plain interesting to know, but I can also plan ahead to give make sure I have enough juice left throughout the day.
 The Anker Prime power isn’t just about a screen though, it also has a solid 20,000mAh of battery which I managed to get a few days' worth of keeping my phone and laptop going with short bursts of recharging, or one big recharge of my MacBook Pro 13. The big 200W maximum output, with a 100W single port output, also allowed me to use my laptop at full power. The power bank is a little boxy for slipping into pockets, but it looks great.
 Read more: Anker Prime 20,000mAh Power Bank (200W) review 
 FAQs 
 Will one of the best portable chargers work for a laptop?
 Sadly not, you will need a power bank with a much higher capacity than most power banks used to charge camera phones or other small appliances. It's recommended that you invest in a power bank with a 20,000 mAh or larger especially if you want to charge it multiple times. 
 How do I connect my laptop to the powerbank?
 How you connect your laptop to your power bank will depend on the time of charging cable your laptop needs. While most modern laptops such as the Apple Macbook Pro 14 M2 will have a USB C input, some older models might still use round AC adapters or a standard USB A input. You will be able to get the correct cable from Amazon.

Shopping for back-to-school? I’d recommend these GaN chargers for saving space and packing more power
From a $9 spare to a $56 desk hub, these chargers cut down on cable clutter so that you can focus on your studies, not how cluttered your desk looks.
By Shikhar Mehrotra Published July 31, 2026
Save
Anker / Amazon

Between a phone, a laptop, a tablet, and perhaps a pair of wireless earbuds that require charging every day or every few days, most students are packing multiple chargers for move-in day. Those big, heavy bricks take up valuable backpack space that could otherwise be free for carrying more items. 

However, GaN chargers fix that problem in two ways. First, they deliver the same amount of power from a much smaller body, thanks to gallium nitride transistors. Furthermore, if you’re willing to spend a little more upfront, you can get a high-capacity, multi-device charger capable of powering your entire digital ecosystem from a single wall outlet, something that could be very useful for a dorm room.

Spigen USB-C 20W GaN Charger

We’ve included Spigen in our charger recommendations over the years, and the 20W GaN charger is no different.

This is the charger that I’d actually buy, in pairs: one for the backpack, one for the nightstand, and one to leave at a parent’s house. Speaking of backpacks, you won’t have a hard time fitting this in, since it’s one of the smallest and the lightest GaN chargers Spigen sells. It also comes with a foldable plug.

And yes, it’s compatible with the latest iPhones, iPads, Samsung or Pixel phones, and basically all other devices that support the USB-C PD standard. However, it isn’t the best option if you’re looking for a phone charger that also doubles as a laptop charger. Last but not least, you don’t get a wire in the box; that’s worth knowing as well.

BUY AT AMAZON

If you only have one power outlet in your dorm room (or you share one with your roommate), the multi-port GaN charger from Ugreen is where I’d point you at. For one, it features three ports, which means it can charge a phone, a pair of earbuds, and a tablet or a Kindle, all at the same time. The list of supported protocols is quite extensive as well: PD, QC, and PPS. 

It’s also available in two rather interesting colors (blue and light pink) rather than the generic black and white, in case you’re building a color-matched setup. Finally, it has a relatively small footprint compared to other multi-port chargers you’d find on the market, especially the regular ones. 

The only con that I’d want you to keep in mind while buying this one is that plugging in three devices will slow down the effective charging speed per device. And no, it still can’t charge your laptop properly.

Affordable enough to buy as a backup

What sold me on the $16.99 Spigen 70W dual USB-C charger is that it’s genuinely a two-in-one, not just in terms of two USB-C power outlets, but the way it can charge both a phone and a laptop from the same wall socket, at the same time. If you live in a dorm room where every outlet is occupied, this one can really help you make the most of a single outlet.

With up to 60W output when using a single port, you can use this one to charge your MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, Dell XPS, or any other USB-C PD-supported device. It won’t push two laptops to full speed at once, but for one laptop (up to 50W) and one phone (up to 20W), it’s a genuinely useful two-outlet-in-one.

It can also charge multiple devices much faster than the Ugreen charger I recommended earlier. You can read about all the configurations (and you must) on the Amazon product page I’ve linked to below. Basically, you can have your laptop plugged into the top-most USB-C port, and your phone and earbuds in the other two, and it will still charge all the devices at a decent speed.

The Ugreen Nexode 100W GaN charger generates enough power to fast-charge a MacBook Air-class laptop with one port (either of the top two) while a phone and a set of headphones top up on the other two. So a student juggling three devices during a study session won’t be stuck rationing outlets. 

Since it’s a multi-port charger, you must go through the power output configuration for when you’re using one or multiple devices. What you should know, however, is that the maximum output while using one device is 100W, but it drops down to 45W while powering four devices.

The folding plug helps ensure the charger survives being tossed loose into a backpack pocket instead of snapping off at the wall prongs. It’s compatible with a variety of USB-C devices as well. If you ask me, I’d get this over carrying two or three separate chargers.

It increases the maximum output power ceiling, from 100W to 140W. In practical terms, you can use the brick to fast-charge two laptops simultaneously. Charge four devices together, and you can still direct a decent 65W to your laptop, 45W to your tablet, and 9W each to your smartphone and earbuds.

So, when your roommate asks for your charger, you can simply ask to use the empty slot in the multi-port charger. This one is around 35% smaller than Apple’s own 140W charging brick, which, by the way, only has a single USB-C output. So it’s convenience and versatility packed in one device.

The Anker Prime is the one purchase that could replace an entire desk’s worth of chargers. It offers four USB-C and two USB-A outlets, giving you the flexibility to plug in up to six devices at once. 

Two of its ports can each push 100W, so two laptops (or a laptop and a high-capacity power bank) can both fast-charge at full speed at the same time, which is genuinely useful for students using heavy gear, like a MacBook Pro or an RTX GeForce-powered Windows laptop. 

At $55.99, it’s the priciest pick here, and it only makes sense once your desk is handling a serious creative or professional workflow, like a dual-laptop setup for part-time content creation or video editing. If you and your roommate are running a tiny makeshift studio, this is the power station I’d go for.

 Maximum single-port charging
 For the highest available output, connect one compatible USB-C PD laptop or other high-power device to USB-C1 or USB-C2 and leave the remaining ports unused. The receiving device requests a supported profile; the charger never forces 100W into equipment that accepts less.
 Not a 100W PPS promise: The manual lists a 100W fixed profile at 20V/5A, while the stated PPS range for C1/C2 is 3.3–21V/3A. Match the device requirement to the actual listed profile.
 Confirm that the device accepts USB-C Power Delivery at the wattage you expect.
 Use a 5A e-marked USB-C-to-USB-C cable for a 20V/5A, 100W path.
 Expect the device, battery temperature and charging controller to reduce power as the battery fills.
 Treat UGREEN timing graphics as laboratory examples, not guaranteed results for every laptop.
 Multi-device charging and power sharing
 One budget, four sockets
 All four ports may be occupied, but the charger has one 100W maximum total. As more devices request power, the internal controller reallocates the budget. The result changes with the active port combination and each device’s requested voltage and current.
 Do not add the labels together: 100W + 100W + 22.5W + 22.5W is not available simultaneously. Those numbers are individual port ceilings under the stated conditions, while the charger itself remains limited to 100W total.
 Place the most power-hungry laptop on USB-C1 or USB-C2.
 Use USB-C3 or USB-A for lower-power phones and accessories when suitable.
 Allow a brief pause or reconnect event when a cable is inserted or removed.
 Check the device’s charging indicator instead of assuming every port retained its solo maximum.
 Why two laptops may charge differently
 Real-world expectations
 Two laptops can have different results even when they appear similar. One may request 20V PD while another reduces input because of battery state, thermal conditions or its manufacturer’s charging policy. Cable capability also matters: a 3A cable cannot provide a 5A path.
 A lower-wattage computer will draw only what it negotiates.
 Charging typically tapers near a high state of charge.
 Heavy computer use can make battery percentage rise more slowly even when input power is substantial.
 Adding a phone or accessory can trigger a new allocation for every active port.
 Compact for a four-port charger—pack the fixed pins carefully
 Physical format
 UGREEN India lists approximate dimensions of 7.6 × 6.9 × 3.3cm and a weight of about 310g. The fixed India plug avoids a separate mains cable, but the body is still a high-power 100W adapter and may be too heavy for a worn or loose socket.
 Travel clarification: The 100–240V input supports many mains systems, but a safe, correctly rated plug adapter may still be required outside India. A shape adapter does not change local electrical rules.
 Use a firm socket that supports the charger without sagging.
 Leave space around the body for airflow.
 Pack it so the fixed pins cannot scratch devices or be bent by pressure.
 For international travel, confirm voltage, frequency, socket shape and adapter quality; input-voltage compatibility does not make the plug fit every country.
 Efficient electronics do not mean “heat-free”
 GaN II and temperature management
 GaN II technology allows a smaller high-power conversion stage, and the gallery presents Thermal Guard monitoring. Some warmth is normal when converting substantial AC power in a compact enclosure, especially with several devices connected.
 Safe interpretation: Thermal monitoring is a protective feature, not permission to block ventilation or continue using damaged equipment.
 Keep the charger uncovered on a hard, open surface.
 Avoid enclosed drawers, bedding, direct sunlight and other heat sources.
 Disconnect it if heat is excessive or accompanied by smell, discoloration, crackling or intermittent power.
 Do not treat the gallery’s efficiency figure as a guaranteed result at every voltage and load.
 Protection features support safe use; they do not replace inspection
 Electrical safeguards
 The gallery identifies overvoltage, overheating, overcurrent and short-circuit protection. These circuits work alongside the connected device’s charging controller and the cable’s rating.
 Never test a protection feature deliberately: Do not short ports, overload extension boards, defeat grounding where required or use the charger in wet locations.
 Inspect the charger, pins, socket and cables before use.
 Keep every connector clean and dry.
 Stop using a cable with exposed conductors, crushed insulation or loose plugs.
 Disconnect the charger during unusual mains behaviour or if protection repeatedly trips.
 Keep liquids, conductive debris and children away from the ports and mains pins.
 Use scenarios
 Where it fits
 The charger is most useful when one wall outlet must cover a changing mix of USB-C and USB-A charging needs.
 Single-laptop desk. Give one compatible laptop priority on C1 or C2, adding other devices only when reduced laptop input is acceptable.
 Office charging point. Keep USB-C and USB-A cables ready for a laptop, phone, headset and other work accessories.
 Family device mix. Charge several lower-power devices while recognising that proprietary fast-charge modes depend on a compatible cable and profile.
 Travel kit consolidation. Replace several adapters when the destination socket and plug-adapter arrangement are safe and properly rated.
 Setup and usability guidance
 From socket to charging
 Troubleshooting order: Test one device at a time on C1 or C2, then substitute a known-good rated cable, then add other devices individually. This separates charger allocation from a cable or device limitation.
 Inspect first. Confirm the fixed pins, casing, wall socket and all device cables are clean, dry and undamaged.
 Use a firm socket. Insert the India plug fully without forcing it, and ensure the charger does not sag or wobble.
 Connect the priority device. Put a high-power USB-C laptop on C1 or C2 with a 5A e-marked cable if up to 100W is required.
 Add lower-power devices deliberately. Use C3 or USB-A when their profiles suit the phone or accessory.
 Wait for renegotiation. After adding or removing a cable, allow the charging indicators to settle before diagnosing a fault.
 Verify actual charging. Check the operating system or a trusted USB power meter if behaviour matters; the front-port label is only a ceiling.
 Disconnect safely. Grip plugs rather than pulling cables, and remove the charger from the socket before cleaning or prolonged storage.
 What this product does
 Clear product boundaries
 Supplies up to 100W from USB-C1 or USB-C2 when either is used alone under compatible conditions.
 Charges as many as four devices from three USB-C ports and one USB-A port.
 Negotiates supported fixed-voltage, PD, PPS and other listed charging profiles.
 Redistributes one shared 100W total as active devices change.
 Provides a compact fixed India-plug solution for home, office and travel use.

 Does not include device charging cables according to the package list.

 Use C1 or C2 for the highest-power USB-C device.

 Keep the charger ventilated and the wall connection firm.

 Add devices one at a time when troubleshooting power sharing.

 Read before connecting

 What “GaN” actually changes 
 GaN means gallium nitride, a semiconductor material used in the charger’s power circuitry. In practical terms, GaN designs can make high-output USB chargers smaller than many older silicon-based designs. That is useful when replacing several laptop, phone, tablet, and accessory adapters with one travel charger.
 GaN is not a charging protocol and is not a guarantee of speed, efficiency, safety, or build quality. The specifications that matter more are:
 USB Power Delivery: the main charging standard for modern USB-C laptops, tablets, and many phones.
 PPS: programmable power supply support, which can matter for Samsung phones and other devices that use variable voltage profiles.
 Output rating: the maximum power available under specified conditions.
 Power allocation: how that output is divided when two, three, or four ports are in use.
 Thermal behavior: whether the charger can maintain useful output or reduces power as it heats up.
 Cable capability: whether the USB-C cable is rated for the power profile you want to use.
 Safety evidence: clear model identification, a reputable seller, warranty information, and an authentic safety mark appropriate for your market.
 USB-IF documentation describes USB Power Delivery and USB-C specifications that support power levels above the earlier 100W ceiling, with USB-C power capability extending to 240W under the relevant specification updates. That does not mean every USB-C device, charger, or cable supports 240W. The device, charger, and cable must negotiate a compatible power profile.

 Apple says a USB-C Mac can be charged with a USB-C power adapter that provides either higher or lower wattage than the recommended adapter, although the charging experience can differ. A higher-rated charger is therefore generally useful for flexibility, but it does not guarantee maximum-speed charging or prevent a demanding laptop from charging slowly under load.
 Why power sharing matters more than peak wattage 
 Manufacturers usually advertise the charger’s maximum total capacity or its best single-port result. Your real-world result depends on which ports are occupied.

 USB PD, PPS, and device compatibility 
 USB Power Delivery
 USB Power Delivery is the baseline to look for when charging USB-C laptops and tablets. A charger with USB-C ports but no suitable PD profile may charge a device slowly, intermittently, or not at all under demanding workloads.
 PPS for Samsung and some other phones
 PPS allows the charger and device to negotiate more granular voltage and current levels. This can matter for Samsung phones that use the company’s higher-speed charging modes. A 100W or 140W label alone does not guarantee Samsung’s fastest mode. The UGREEN Nexode 140W specifically advertises Samsung 45W Super Fast Charging 2.0, but the claim is model- and cable-dependent.
 Laptop model and cable conditions
 Compatibility claims such as a MacBook reaching a particular percentage in 30 minutes should be read as conditional manufacturer claims, not promises for every MacBook. Battery level, temperature, workload, cable rating, and other connected devices all affect the result.
 Do you need a special USB-C cable? 
 For ordinary phone charging, a basic USB-C cable may be sufficient. For 100W-plus charging, cable capability becomes a purchase criterion.
 USB-IF says compliant USB-C-to-USB-C cable categories must be labeled for 60W or 240W power capability with the relevant power icon or logo. Some higher-power profiles also require a 5A electronically marked cable. A generic cable, or a cable included with a phone, should not automatically be assumed to support a 140W charger’s maximum output.
 If you are buying a PD 3.1 charger for a high-power laptop, look for a clearly identified 240W USB-C cable or another cable whose labeled capability meets your device and charger requirements. Also confirm that the cable is USB-C to USB-C; USB-A cables do not provide the same high-power USB-C PD path.
 A high-rated cable does not make an incompatible device charge faster. It only removes the cable as a bottleneck when the charger and device already support the relevant profile.
